title: Karnataka Must Move From an IT Workforce to an Imagination Workforce, Bengaluru Summit Hears
excerpt: A keynote by Astra Studios founder Biren Ghose at the Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 argued that creativity, original intellectual property and human imagination are Karnataka's next workforce advantage in an AI-enabled economy.
body:
• A keynote titled 'From Workforce to Imagination Force' at the Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 made the case that Karnataka must move from an IT workforce to an imagination workforce, built on creativity, original intellectual property and human imagination in an AI-enabled economy.
  • The keynote was delivered by Biren Ghose, founder and chief executive of Astra Studios, on the summit's final day, November 5, according to the summit's published outcomes reports.
  • The three-day summit, held November 3-5 at The Lalit Ashok in Bengaluru under the theme 'Workforce 2030: Scale, Systems, Synergy', drew a footfall of 9,500, with Japan as country partner.
  • On November 4, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar launched Yuva Udyoga Sethu, a digital employment platform for young jobseekers in Karnataka.

Karnataka built its global reputation on the scale of its technology workforce. At the Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 this week, one of the closing arguments was that scale is no longer enough: the state must transition from an IT workforce to an imagination workforce. The argument headlined a keynote titled 'From Workforce to Imagination Force' by Biren Ghose, founder and chief executive officer of Astra Studios, which examined the growing role of creativity, original intellectual property and human imagination in an AI-enabled economy, according to Skill Reporter's summit report and the National Skills Network's outcomes summary.

Why imagination, and why now

The logic running through the summit was that artificial intelligence changes what employers pay a premium for. A fireside discussion moderated by Sanjeev Kumar Gupta, chief executive of the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), brought together Vivek Raghavan and Ankush Sabharwal to discuss how AI can augment workers rather than replace them, with a focus on domain-specific skilling, industry-academia collaboration and continuous learning. Gupta put the shift plainly:

"The most valuable worker is not the one who is competing with AI, but the one who is working alongside AI."

— Sanjeev Kumar Gupta, CEO, Karnataka Digital Economy Mission

Ghose's keynote applied the same reasoning to creative work: as AI tools take over routine production, the scarce skills become originating ideas, owning intellectual property and imagining products and stories that did not exist before. For a state whose technology sector was built on delivering services for clients elsewhere, that is a different economic proposition — one based on creating and owning, not only executing.

The summit around the keynote

The second Bengaluru Skill Summit ran from November 3 to 5 at The Lalit Ashok, Bengaluru. It was organised by the Government of Karnataka's Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood, hosted by the Karnataka Skill Development Corporation, in association with the Karnataka Skill Development Authority, with KDEM as knowledge partner. The summit recorded a footfall of 9,500 and had Japan as its country partner, under the theme 'Workforce 2030: Scale, Systems, Synergy'.

Its programme ran on four tracks — Emerging Skills, Skills for All, Innovation and Global Skills — covering AI and Industry 4.0 jobs, inclusion for women, youth, informal and gig workers, and preparation for overseas employment, including in the care economy. On November 4, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar launched Yuva Udyoga Sethu, a digital employment platform intended to connect skilled young jobseekers in Karnataka with employers. The same day, a Skillathon competition on labour-market intelligence was won by InUnity – Innovation for Community, from Mangaluru.

What it means for Karnataka's tech workers

For the diaspora engineers and designers who came up through Bengaluru's IT industry, the message from the summit is familiar in direction but sharper in wording: routine coding and delivery skills are being repriced by AI, and the state's skilling machinery — its skill development corporation, digital economy mission and new jobs platform — is being pointed at AI-era roles, creative industries and global mobility. Whether training programmes can actually produce an 'imagination workforce' at the scale Karnataka produced software engineers is the unproven part. The summit set the ambition; the follow-through will be visible in what the state's skilling programmes teach next, and what employers hire for.
nri_angle: Many diaspora tech workers built careers in Bengaluru's IT services industry; Karnataka's push toward creative, IP-owning AI-era work signals how the jobs they left — and may return to — are changing.
author: Diaspora Desk

items.text: AI tools to augment rather than replace workers.
Focus on creativity and original intellectual property.
